title: Ports: Many Doors, One Address
about: How one address can run many services at once.

cards.prompt:
One [[server]] runs a website, email and a game, all on one [[IP address]].

What else does a [[packet]] need to reach the right **program**?

options.text: A number saying which program it's for
Every program gets a copy and ignores the rest
options.nudge: Copying every packet to every program would be slow, and anyone could read anything.

options.text: Nothing: each program has its own IP address
options.nudge: Here all three share one IP address, so the address alone can't pick between them.

options.text: It goes to whichever program is least busy
options.nudge: A game can't make sense of an email: the packet has to say where it belongs.

cards.explanation: Every packet also carries a number that picks the program: a **port**. The IP address finds the computer, and the port finds the program.
cards.hint: The IP address is the same for all three, so what could tell them apart?

cards.title: Ports are like apartment numbers
cards.body:
The street address gets a letter to the **building**; the apartment number gets it to the right **door**.

The [[IP address]] is the building and a **port** is the door: each program **listens** on its own. Websites use port `80`, secure ones ([[HTTPS]]) `443`, written `198.51.100.10:443`.

options.text: Port 443: the door for the secure website program
A fifth octet, making the IP address longer
options.nudge: IPv4 always has exactly four octets: the colon starts something separate.

options.text: The packet may pass through up to 443 routers
options.nudge: Routers get it to the computer: this number is about what happens once it's there.

options.text: The server will answer within 443 milliseconds
options.nudge: Nothing in an address measures time: which program should the packet reach?

cards.explanation: After the colon comes the **port**: 443 is the standard one for secure websites ([[HTTPS]]). It isn't part of the IP address, which always has four octets.
cards.hint: The IP address is the building: what does the number after the colon pick out?

cards.prompt: Your end uses a temporary [[port]], like `51544`. In `netstat -n`, **Local Address** is your end; **Foreign Address** is the other. Run it.
cards.intro:
Microsoft Windows [simulated Command Prompt]
Type help to see the commands you can use here.

commands.output:
Active Connections

  Proto  Local Address          Foreign Address        State
  TCP    192.168.1.42:51544     198.51.100.10:443      ESTABLISHED
  TCP    192.168.1.42:51547     203.0.113.80:80        ESTABLISHED

success.question: Which port on 198.51.100.10 is the laptop connected to?

cards.explanation: Under **Foreign Address**, `198.51.100.10:443` means port **443**, a secure website; `51544` is the laptop's temporary port. The second line has its own temporary port, so replies never mix up.
cards.hint: Find the line with `198.51.100.10` and read the number after its colon under **Foreign Address**.
cards.nudge: **Local Address** is your laptop's end: the server's port is under **Foreign Address**.

cards.prompt: **NAT** swaps your private address and port for the router's public one and a port it picks, noting the pair in a **NAT table**. Order the steps.
cards.explanation: The router rewrites the sender on the way **out** and records it, so the server replies to `203.0.113.7:40001`. The port then tells the router which device the reply is for.
cards.hint: Follow one [[packet]] out and its reply back: a table entry is written before it's read.
cards.nudge: The server only ever sees the router's public address and port: what must happen first?

cards.prompt:
The [[router]]'s [[NAT]] table says:

- `203.0.113.7:40001` → `192.168.1.20:51000`
- `203.0.113.7:40002` → `192.168.1.21:51000`

A reply arrives for `203.0.113.7:40002`. Which device gets it? Type the **last number** of its [[private address]].
cards.explanation: Port **40002** maps to `192.168.1.21:51000`, so the device ending in **21** gets it. Both used port 51000, but their different public ports keep the replies apart.
cards.hint: Find the line matching the reply's public address and [[port]], then read its private address.
cards.nudge: Both laptops use port 51000, so look at the router's public port in the reply.

cards.prompt: Two laptops at home both use port **51000** for one website. How does the [[router]] tell their replies apart?

options.text: Each gets its own public port, like 40001
It can't: one fails until the other ends
options.nudge: Many devices share one router fine: what does the router choose when it rewrites the sender?

options.text: It sends each reply to both laptops
options.nudge: The NAT table sends each reply to exactly one device: what could make the replies differ?

options.text: The server adds the private address
options.nudge: The server never sees private addresses: the answer is in the router's own table.

cards.explanation: The router picks a **different public port** for each conversation, so replies arrive on different ports and its NAT table knows whose each one is. The server never learns the private addresses.
cards.hint: The router picks the public port for each conversation: what could it do differently for each laptop?

cards.title: Recap
cards.body:
- The [[IP address]] finds the computer; the **port** finds the program.
- Websites use port 80; secure websites use 443.
- Your router's **NAT table** uses ports to route each reply home.

Next: two ways to deliver data, TCP and UDP.
